cells.tense: This careful thought is here now, and the pen is in your hand.
cells.act: keep building the thing with sustained craft
cells.ask: Take a piece of a practice you belong to — a recipe, a repair, some wording — and add one more round of work to it before the week is out.
cells.core:
When something matters and its shape has been settled over time, you can work out what belongs inside it and what does not. You hold how it is done against how it ought to be done, and the thing comes out truer than it started. Sorting like that is what keeps a shared practice worth passing on.

Where it is going well, you can afford to stay at the bench. Take one piece of it — a recipe, a repair, wording, an old way of doing a job — and give it today's part instead of the whole restoration. Small repeated work is how anything gets deep, and there is no way around it. What you sharpen slowly can then be used by someone else.
cells.sheetLine: You sharpen what is shared until it holds.
cells.place: where what is handed down between generations is kept, used and taught

cells.tense: You are already braced for a version of this that has not arrived.
cells.act: make the sacrifice visible without explaining it
cells.ask: One job you normally do unseen for your group, do it where whoever it is for can watch, and say nothing about it.
cells.core:
You read what belongs in a joint practice faster than you can say it, and under that speed the case gets argued ahead of time, before anybody has raised it. Care turns into defending a position nobody has taken. You are sharpening against a critique that lives only in your own head, and the shared thing you love gets handled like a problem to win.

Put one piece of the work in the open instead. Do the cooking, the setting up, the careful correction while the person it serves is watching, and say nothing about it. If thanks come, take them without deflecting. Nothing needs explaining. The need to be right in advance is the only thing worth putting down, and there is nothing to lose by it.
cells.sheetLine: You argue with a critique no one has made yet.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that is already behind you.
cells.act: let the exchange with someone run both ways
cells.ask: Notice something someone gave you lately, then give back a thing of the same size — no more, no less, no tally kept after.
cells.core:
The careful private sorting still happens, but what you arrive at stays private; none of it gets used to fix anything between people. You can see what the shared way of doing things has been missing, and it stays a seeing. The give and take around you keeps moving without you in it.

Getting the habit back does not work by trying harder to understand what you all do. It works through one small exchange. Recall something someone gave you, match it with something you give back, and make that swap where the person you owe can watch it happen. Fairness returns through use; your eye is not the thing that is missing.
cells.sheetLine: You see what is missing from the exchange and stay out of it.

cells.tense: The pen is down in a room where you are already writing.
cells.act: walk through the thing you built and touch nothing
cells.ask: Move through a shared thing you helped make — a meal, a place, a gathering — taking it as it stands, fixing nothing.
cells.core:
The refining is carrying the shared practice — the language, the way a thing gets done, the correction quietly made — and if someone asked who set it up, you would say the group did. Your hand is in it more than you have let yourself see, and what you have made is running right now with your name filed nowhere.

One pass through it brings your part back. Move through what you helped make, enjoy it, change nothing, improve nothing, and take it as enough the way it stands. If you stayed a while and it turned out well, notice what you had to do with that. What you leave untended this once can be the thing your own work still holds.
cells.sheetLine: Your part in what is shared has gone unnamed.

attempts.check: The record does not say the person is the one who made or kept the traditions in front of them — only that this kind of careful, private sorting is happening there now. A reader could reasonably object that they are in culture, not its author, and the sharp eye is turned on everything else rather than on what has been handed down. The asks survive being wrong because each only asks for one piece of work or one exchange with a real person, which is worth doing whether or not the reading is right. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line claiming they built the custom they may have simply inherited — that one is cut.

The sentence that serves me more than them is any line that awards them authorship of something they merely inherited; it is gone.
